references.text: The introduction of Babylon in Nimrod's kingdom as a central place for the events in chapter 11.
In Peleg's days the earth was divided - a reference to the scattering of the nations after Babel.
The background to the confusion of languages: the whole earth had one language, and the people tried to build a city and a tower to make a name for themselves.
The Most High distributed their inheritances among the nations and separated the children of Adam from each other - linked to the scattering from Babel.
Pentecost as a reversal of Babel's confusion, where people from different nations understand the apostles' speech in their own language.
Babel used as a symbol of a morally and spiritually corrupt society, in contrast to the original city of Babel where the confusion of languages took place.
Further development of Babel as a symbol of judgment and destruction.
Theological contrast: Babylon as the starting point for God's scattering of peoples (Genesis) becomes captivity for Babylon itself (Jeremiah).
Narrative arc: From Babylon as the center of human gathering and scattering (Genesis) to Babylon as an eternally desolate place (Jeremiah).
Thematic parallel: Babel's 'voice' that was confused in Genesis is silenced in Jeremiah as the fulfillment of God's judgment.
Theological connection: Babylon's judgment in Jeremiah is directly linked to its violence against the nations it scattered in Genesis.
